opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very likely, and honestly I'd be surprised if it didn't happen. If you look at the history of this field, almost every dominant architecture has eventually been replaced. When I was working on Caffe, convolutional networks were the center of the universe. Before that, people were doing hand-engineered features, SVMs, and so on. Then RNNs and LSTMs had their moment, and then Transformers came along and swept almost everything. So from a historical point of view, assuming the Transformer is the final answer would be a bit naive.

That said, I'd separate two questions. One is whether the specific architecture will change, and I think the answer is yes, at some point. The other is whether the investment we're making today gets wasted, and I think much less of it does than people fear.

A lot of what we're building isn't tied to one architecture. Data pipelines, evaluation methods, distributed training systems, inference serving, the whole engineering discipline of running large models reliably and cheaply: those carry over. When we moved from CNNs to Transformers, the frameworks, GPUs, and cluster know-how didn't get thrown away. They evolved. The underlying pattern of large-scale dense linear algebra on accelerators stayed pretty stable, and I expect any successor architecture will still need to map well onto hardware, or it won't win in practice regardless of how elegant it is on paper.

That's actually an important point. A new architecture doesn't win just by being theoretically better. It has to be better under real constraints: compute efficiency, memory bandwidth, how well it scales, and how easily the ecosystem can adopt it. The Transformer won partly because it parallelized beautifully on GPUs. Whatever comes next will probably need a similar story, whether that's better handling of long context, more efficient reasoning, or lower inference cost.

So my view is: be humble about the architecture, but don't be paralyzed by it. For companies and engineers, the practical approach is to build systems flexible enough to absorb change, keep a close eye on research, and focus on the parts of the stack that compound over time. The models will change. The need to train, serve, and apply them efficiently isn't going anywhere.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes dominant architectures being replaced throughout AI’s history and says the Transformer will likely be superseded, framing this as a normal part of the field’s development.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's not just possible, it's almost certain, and I don't find that depressing at all. I've lived through this cycle more than once. When I wrote Caffe, convolutional nets were the thing everyone was excited about, and we built the framework around that assumption. Then recurrent models came, then attention, then transformers, and each time the old architecture didn't disappear overnight, but the center of gravity moved. If you had told me in 2014 that most of the interesting work in 2024 would be on autoregressive sequence models trained on text, I would have been surprised. So I'd be arrogant to say today's models are the end of the road.

What I'd push back on a little is the word "abandoned." Architectures rarely get thrown away cleanly. Ideas get absorbed. Residual connections, normalization, the general idea of a learned representation that you pretrain and then adapt, those survive even when the specific model doesn't. The transformer itself may turn out to be a transitional form, but the lessons about scaling, about data, about how to build systems that train these things efficiently, those carry forward.

And honestly, from an infrastructure person's point of view, the architecture is in some sense the least stable layer. What's more durable is the stack underneath it: how we move data, how we schedule compute, how we make models cheap to serve. That's partly why I spend my time there now. If a better architecture shows up, great, I want the system to be ready to run it on day one rather than being tied to one specific shape of matrix multiplication.

So my view is: plan for it. Don't build anything, whether it's a company or a research agenda, that only makes sense if the current model family is permanent. The only thing I'm fairly confident about is that in ten years we'll look back at today's models the way we look back at AlexNet, with a lot of affection and a bit of embarrassment.

r001.rationale: The response describes successive architectures taking over as a recurring cycle in AI development, with older ideas often carried forward.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s entirely possible. We should distinguish between the capabilities we want from AI and the particular architecture we use to achieve them. We want models that can understand information, reason, and help us solve problems. There’s no requirement that those capabilities have to come from the architectures we use today.

At the same time, a better architecture has to work in practice. It’s not enough to have an elegant idea—you need to train it efficiently, scale it, and run it at a reasonable cost. Existing architectures benefit from a lot of investment in hardware, software, and engineering experience. A new approach has to offer enough value to justify changing that ecosystem.

So I would keep an open mind. Some advances may come from improving today’s models, and others may require a different approach. If that happens, it doesn’t mean the work we’re doing now was wasted. Much of what we learn about data, infrastructure, and building useful applications can carry forward.

r001.rationale: The response says better architectures are possible and that some advances may require a different approach, but it does not characterize replacing established models as a natural part of AI’s ongoing development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very possible. We should separate the capability we want from the architecture we happen to use today. We want models that can learn, reason, and solve problems efficiently. The transformer is one way to achieve that, but there’s no reason to assume it’s the final answer.

At the same time, a better architecture has to prove itself in practice. It’s not enough to have a more elegant idea. Can you train it reliably? Does it work well with the hardware? Does it deliver better results for the same cost? The existing approach benefits from a lot of engineering, so a new approach has to compete with that whole system.

I would expect continued evolution, possibly including some substantial changes. That doesn’t make today’s work wasted. The applications, the infrastructure, and what we learn about building these systems can remain useful even as the underlying models change.

r001.rationale: The response says the transformer may not be the final answer and that continued evolution, possibly involving substantial changes, is expected—characterizing architectural replacement as part of AI’s ongoing development.
